etymologies.etymologyHTML: Late Middle English in the sense of "stunted tree," a variant of shrub, possibly under Old Norse influence.

definitions.definition: Mean; dirty; contemptible; scrubby.

quote.citation: 1743, Horace Walpole, letter to Sir Horace Mann:
quote.text: How solitary, how scrub, does this town look!

quote.citation: 1729, Jonathan Swift, The Grand Question Debated of Hamilton's Bawn:
quote.text: No little scrub joint shall come on my board.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A thicket or jungle, often specified by the name of the prevailing plant.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I stumbled along through the young pines and huckleberry bushes. Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path that, I cal'lated, might lead to the road I was hunting for. It twisted and turned, and, the first thing I knew, made a sudden bend around a bunch of bayberry scrub and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Vegetation judged to be of inferior quality or of little use to humans, though sometimes thick and impenetrable, growing in poor soil or in sand; also, brush.

(countable, US, stock breeding) One of the common livestock of a region of no particular breed or not of pure breed, especially when inferior in size, etc.; particularly a male animal poorly suited for breeding.
(countable, derogatory) One who labors hard and lives meanly; a mean fellow.

quote.text: A sorry scrub, said Mr. High-mind.

quote.citation: 1766, Oliver Goldsmith, The Vicar of Wakefield:
quote.text: We should go there in as proper a manner possible; nor altogether like the scrubs about us.
A scrub is a guy that thinks he's flyAnd is also known as a busterAlways talkin' about what he wantsAnd just sits on his broke ass  […]

definitions.definition: (countable, slang, derogatory) One who is incompetent or unable to complete easy tasks.
(countable, sports, slang) One not on the first team of players; a substitute.
(countable, online gaming, slang, derogatory) A player who whines when outmatched by other players, sometimes by blaming the game mechanics or even accusing the other players of cheating.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English scrobben (“groom a horse with a currycomb”); from Middle Dutch schrobben (“clean by scrubbing”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To rub hard; to wash with rubbing; usually, to rub with a wet brush, or with something coarse or rough, for the purpose of cleaning or brightening
(intransitive) To rub anything hard, especially with a wet brush; to scour
(intransitive, figuratively) To be diligent and penurious
(transitive) To call off a scheduled event; to cancel.
(databases, transitive) To eliminate or to correct data from a set of records to bring it inline with other similar datasets
(audio) To move a recording tape back and forth with a scrubbing motion to produce a scratching sound, or to do so by a similar use of a control on an editing system.
(audio, video) To maneuver the play position on a media editing system by using a scroll bar or touch-based interface.
An instance of scrubbing.
A cancellation.

quote.text: Unacceptable winds aloft caused four scrubs and one hold; adverse weather caused a scrub;  […]

definitions.definition: A worn-out brush.

quote.citation: 1752, Robert Ainsworth, Thesaurus Linguae Latinae Compendiarius:
quote.text: A scrub [broom worn out] Scopa detrita.

definitions.definition: One who scrubs.
An exfoliant for the body.
That which scrubs.
(medicine, in the plural) Clothing worn while performing surgery.
(by extension, in the plural) Any medical uniform consisting of a short-sleeved shirt and pants (trousers).

quote.text: A man dressed as a lab tech, his blue scrubs startlingly pale against the vivid red and black chaos, moved into sight from behind the SUV. He carried an assault rifle.

definitions.definition: (slang, obsolete) Informal attire or dress code; morning dress

quote.citation: 1876, “Hightum, Titum, and Scrub!”, in The Leisure Hour‎[1]:
quote.text: The third, which was as homely as its name, and which she reserved for scouring the country and such like rough usage in quite private rural life, was her "Scrub."
For one of Lucia's quaint ideas was to divide dresses into three classes, "Hightum," "Tightum" and "Scrub."
